title: Non-Commutative Cramer's Rule via Quasideterminants
description: Extends Cramer's Rule to division rings using the Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminant. For 2×2 systems Ax = b, the solution x₀ = |A|₀₀⁻¹·(b₀ - a₀₁·a₁₁⁻¹·b₁) is proved correct, unique, and shown to reduce to classical Cramer's Rule when D is commutative.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified over any DivisionRing D.
originalContributions: Defined quasidet₀₀ and quasidet₁₁: Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminants for 2×2 matrices
Defined ncSolve: explicit solution formula for non-commutative 2×2 systems
Proved ncSolve_row0 and ncSolve_row1: correctness of each row equation
Proved nc_cramers_rule: the main theorem Ax = b via mulVec over DivisionRing
Proved nc_kernel_trivial: the kernel is trivial when quasideterminant is invertible
Proved quasidet_mul_eq_det: commutative reduction to classical determinant

sections.title: Quasideterminants
sections.summary: Defines the (0,0) and (1,1) quasideterminants for 2×2 matrices over a division ring. The (0,0)-quasideterminant $|A|_{00} = a_{00} - a_{01} \cdot a_{11}^{-1} \cdot a_{10}$ is the Schur complement of the (1,1)-entry.
sections.mathContext: The $(i,j)$-quasideterminant of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ is the Schur complement obtained by 'eliminating' the complementary row and column: $|A|_{00} = a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10}$ and $|A|_{11} = a_{11} - a_{10}a_{00}^{-1}a_{01}$. In a commutative ring, both equal $\det(A)/a_{jj}$, but in general they differ because $a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10} \neq a_{10}a_{11}^{-1}a_{01}$.

sections.title: Solution Formula
sections.summary: Defines `ncSolve`: the non-commutative Cramer solution $x_0 = |A|_{00}^{-1} \cdot (b_0 - a_{01} \cdot a_{11}^{-1} \cdot b_1)$ and $x_1 = a_{11}^{-1} \cdot (b_1 - a_{10} \cdot x_0)$.
sections.mathContext: The solution formula arises from Gaussian elimination applied non-commutatively: row 1 gives $x_1 = a_{11}^{-1}(b_1 - a_{10}x_0)$, and substituting into row 0 yields $(a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10})x_0 = b_0 - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}b_1$, so $x_0 = |A|_{00}^{-1}(b_0 - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}b_1)$. Note that all inverses multiply on the left, matching the convention $\sum_j a_{ij}x_j = b_i$.

sections.title: Correctness
sections.summary: Proves row correctness: `ncSolve_row1` uses left cancellation $a_{11} \cdot a_{11}^{-1} = 1$; `ncSolve_row0` factors out the quasideterminant and cancels $q \cdot q^{-1} = 1$.
sections.mathContext: Row 1: $a_{10}x_0 + a_{11} \cdot a_{11}^{-1}(b_1 - a_{10}x_0) = a_{10}x_0 + b_1 - a_{10}x_0 = b_1$. Row 0 is harder: after distributing and regrouping, $(a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10})x_0 + a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}b_1 = |A|_{00} \cdot |A|_{00}^{-1}(b_0 - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}b_1) + a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}b_1 = b_0$. The non-commutativity makes the factoring step $a_{00}x_0 - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10}x_0 = (a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10})x_0$ nontrivial — it requires `sub_mul` in a non-commutative ring.

sections.title: Main Theorem
sections.summary: **nc_cramers_rule**: proves $A \cdot \text{ncSolve}(A, b) = b$ over any division ring $D$ via `mulVec` with componentwise verification.

sections.title: Uniqueness
sections.summary: Proves kernel triviality (`nc_kernel_trivial`) and solution uniqueness (`nc_cramers_unique`): if $|A|_{00} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 0$, the solution is unique.
sections.mathContext: Kernel triviality: $Ax = 0 \implies x = 0$ by Gaussian elimination in reverse — extract $x_1$ from row 1, substitute into row 0 to get $|A|_{00} \cdot x_0 = 0$, then use the division ring property ($ab = 0 \implies a = 0 \lor b = 0$) to conclude $x_0 = 0$, whence $x_1 = 0$. Uniqueness follows: if $Ax = b$ and $Ay = b$, then $A(x-y) = 0$, so $x = y$.

sections.title: Commutative Reduction
sections.summary: Shows `quasidet_mul_eq_det`: over a field, $|A|_{00} \cdot a_{11} = \det(A)$, recovering classical Cramer's Rule.
sections.mathContext: Over a commutative field $F$: $|A|_{00} \cdot a_{11} = (a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10}) \cdot a_{11} = a_{00}a_{11} - a_{01}a_{10} = \det(A)$. This shows the quasideterminant is $\det(A)/a_{11}$ when entries commute, recovering the classical Cramer formula $x_i = \det(A_i)/\det(A)$ as a special case.

overview.historicalContext:
Gabriel Cramer published his rule for solving linear systems via determinants in 1750, but the formula $x_i = \det(A_i)/\det(A)$ fundamentally requires that the entries commute — the classical determinant $\sum_{\sigma} \text{sgn}(\sigma) \prod a_{i,\sigma(i)}$ is ill-defined when multiplication order matters.

The problem of extending linear algebra to non-commutative settings arose naturally in quantum mechanics (where observables are operators on Hilbert space) and in the study of division rings like Hamilton's quaternions $\mathbb{H}$ (1843). Dieudonné (1943) introduced a determinant for matrices over division rings, but it takes values in the abelianization $D^\times/[D^\times, D^\times]$, losing the ability to solve systems directly.

Israel Gelfand and Vladimir Retakh transformed the subject with their theory of quasideterminants, introduced in 'Determinants of matrices over noncommutative rings' (1991) and developed systematically in 'Quasideterminants, I' (1997). Their key insight: instead of a single determinant, an $n \times n$ matrix has $n^2$ quasideterminants, one for each entry. The $(i,j)$-quasideterminant is the Schur complement of the complementary $(n{-}1) \times (n{-}1)$ submatrix — for $2 \times 2$ matrices, $|A|_{00} = a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10}$. Unlike Dieudonné's determinant, quasideterminants take values in the ring itself and directly yield solution formulas.

The Gelfand-Retakh theory proved remarkably fertile: quasideterminants connect to the theory of free fields (Cohn, 1995), appear in the study of quantum groups (Manin, 1988), play a role in non-commutative symmetric functions (Gelfand et al., 2005), and underlie non-commutative algebraic geometry. The quasideterminant-based Cramer's Rule formalized here is the simplest instance of this rich framework.
overview.problemStatement: Can Cramer's Rule extend to non-commutative settings using quasideterminants?
overview.text: A complete formalization of Cramer's Rule for $2 \times 2$ systems $Ax = b$ over an arbitrary division ring $D$, using the Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminant $|A|_{00} = a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10}$ as the non-commutative analogue of the determinant. The proof proceeds by explicit back-substitution: solve row 1 for $x_1$, substitute into row 0, and factor out the quasideterminant to solve for $x_0$. The file proves three key properties — correctness ($A \cdot \text{ncSolve}(A,b) = b$), uniqueness (kernel triviality implies the solution is unique), and commutative reduction ($|A|_{00} \cdot a_{11} = \det(A)$ over a field). All 8 theorems are fully verified with 0 sorries and 0 axioms over the Lean 4 `DivisionRing` typeclass, which covers quaternions, skew fields, and any non-commutative division algebra.
overview.proofStrategy: Define the solution via Gaussian elimination (back-substitution from row 2, then use quasideterminant for row 1). Prove correctness by verifying each row equation using left cancellation (a·a⁻¹ = 1). Prove uniqueness via kernel triviality (q·x = 0, q ≠ 0 ⟹ x = 0 in a division ring).
keyInsights: The quasideterminant is the Schur complement: |A|₀₀ = a₀₀ - a₀₁·a₁₁⁻¹·a₁₀
Non-commutativity means left and right cancellation must be carefully tracked
The solution formula uses left multiplication by inverses, matching the row structure of Ax = b
Over a commutative field, |A|₀₀ · a₁₁ = det(A), recovering the classical formula
Kernel triviality exploits the division ring property that $ab = 0 \implies a = 0 \lor b = 0$ (no zero divisors), which is the algebraic core distinguishing division rings from general rings
prerequisites: Linear algebra (matrix-vector multiplication, systems of equations)
Division rings: rings where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse, but multiplication need not commute (e.g., quaternions $\mathbb{H}$)
Schur complement: the matrix identity $A/D = A - BD^{-1}C$ for block matrices

conclusion.summary: Cramer's Rule fully extends to 2×2 systems over division rings via quasideterminants. The formalization proves correctness, uniqueness, and commutative reduction with 0 sorries and 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications:
This validates the Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminant framework as the correct non-commutative analogue of determinants for solving linear systems. The quasideterminant $|A|_{00} = a_{00} - a_{01}a_{11}^{-1}a_{10}$ plays the role of $\det(A)$ in non-commutative settings: when it is invertible, the system has a unique solution.

**Connections to broader mathematics:**

1. BLOCK MATRIX INVERSION: The Schur complement $A - BD^{-1}C$ for block matrices $\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}$ is exactly the quasideterminant in the $2 \times 2$ block case. This connects to the Woodbury identity, the matrix inversion lemma, and Kalman filtering.

2. QUANTUM GROUPS: Manin's quantum matrices (1988) satisfy non-commutative relations $ab = qba$. Quasideterminants provide the correct notion of 'determinant' for these $q$-deformed algebras, where the classical determinant has no natural analogue.

3. FREE PROBABILITY: In Voiculescu's free probability theory, quasideterminants appear in the study of free random variables and non-commutative power series. The connection to free fields (Cohn, Amitsur) makes quasideterminants a bridge between algebra and operator theory.

4. QUATERNIONIC LINEAR ALGEBRA: The quaternions $\mathbb{H}$ are the most important concrete division ring. This formalization immediately applies to quaternionic systems arising in computer graphics (rotation composition), robotics (spatial transformations), and signal processing (quaternionic Fourier analysis).
openQuestions: Can this be generalized to $n \times n$ matrices using the full quasideterminant theory? For $n > 2$, the quasideterminant $|A|_{ij}$ is defined recursively via $(n{-}1) \times (n{-}1)$ Schur complements: $|A|_{ij} = a_{ij} - r_i A_{ij}^{-1} c_j$ where $r_i, c_j$ are the deleted row/column and $A_{ij}$ is the complementary submatrix. The recursive structure makes the $n \times n$ case substantially harder to formalize.

What is the relationship between quasideterminants and the Dieudonné determinant for $n \times n$ matrices over division rings? Dieudonné's determinant maps to $D^\times/[D^\times, D^\times] \cup \{0\}$ and detects invertibility, while quasideterminants take values in $D$ itself. For $2 \times 2$ matrices, $\text{Ddet}(A) = |A|_{00} \cdot a_{11} \bmod [D^\times, D^\times]$. Can this relationship be formalized in Lean?

Can the proof technique extend to concrete quaternionic linear systems $Ax = b$ where $A \in M_2(\mathbb{H})$? Lean's Mathlib provides `Quaternion` — instantiating `DivisionRing` for quaternions and running the formalized solver would yield a verified quaternionic Cramer's Rule applicable to rotation composition and spatial kinematics.
